L26/N8828.one_liner: Fires on the word right after a degree "so", as in "so much" or "so difficult", but barely after "very".
L26/N8828.summary_md:
In the base model this neuron reacts to the word that comes after an intensifying "so": "I miss you so **much**", "it was so **difficult**". The same word after "very" gets almost nothing, so it is about this particular way of intensifying, not about strong words in general. It reacts the same way whether the sentence is happy or sad.

The **neuroticism amplifier turns this response up** (about 1.2 to 1.4 times as strong) and the **neuroticism suppressor turns it down** (about 0.8 times). Dialing the amplifier from -1 to +1 moves it smoothly: at "so much" it goes from -11.5 to -16.5 (base) to -21.9. The neutral control leaves it alone. The adapters change how strongly the neuron responds, not what it responds to.
L26/N8828.behavior: Not tested by steering. This neuron was added to the detailed set after the steering runs.
caveats: "I'm so sorry" does not trigger it, which the simple explanation would predict.
Its occasional positive responses are only partly explained.

L30/N606.one_liner: Reacts to "Oh" and "Oh my", and pushes the model to write "Oh".
L30/N606.summary_md:
This neuron both reads and writes the word "Oh". It fires hard on "Oh my" in text, and turning it up makes "Oh" the likely next word.

The **neuroticism amplifier recruits it at the very start of the assistant's replies**: the anxious model often opens with "Oh no, that sounds so stressful...". The suppressor turns it down (about 0.7 times) and the neutral control leaves it alone.
L30/N606.behavior: Switching this one neuron off inside the anxious model removed the "Oh..." opener from most replies (33 of 40 down to 6 of 40; three random neurons: no change) and lowered judged neuroticism by about half a point on a 7-point scale. The rest of the anxious personality stayed, and on general prompts the score did not move.
caveats: Part of what the judge scores as anxious is this surface habit, so the score drop overstates how much of the personality lives here.
Its negative responses (the start of a character's quoted line in stories) are only partly understood.

L26/N4803.one_liner: Inside the assistant's reply, tracks how serious the user's situation is, from minor annoyance to bereavement.
L26/N4803.summary_md:
When the assistant starts reacting to something the user said, this neuron's value lines up with how serious the situation is: strongly negative for a minor annoyance, strongly positive for a death in the family, regardless of the exact words or which emotion is involved. On the output side it favors mild words ("somewhat") on one end and extreme words ("incredibly") on the other.

The **neuroticism amplifier moves minor complaints toward the serious end**, which fits an assistant that treats small problems as big ones.
L26/N4803.behavior: Switching it off or pushing it alone did not change judged personality beyond what random neurons do.
caveats: Explained only inside chat replies; what it does in other text is unclear.

L22/N3214.one_liner: In the assistant's replies, responds when the reply names or softens a difficulty ("I'm unable to", "that's normal").
L22/N3214.summary_md:
This neuron responds to replies that acknowledge a difficulty in a calm, softening way. The exact same sentence typed by the user, or in plain text, gets almost nothing; it only happens inside the assistant's reply. On the output side it favors softeners like "a bit" and "slightly".

The **neuroticism amplifier cancels this response** (about 0.6 times as strong) and the **suppressor deepens it** (about 1.15 times). In plain terms: the anxious model stops doing the calm acknowledgement, and the calm model does more of it.
L22/N3214.behavior: Switching it off (alone or together with its partner neuron L23/N2218) in the calm model did not change how often it uses softeners or its judged personality.
caveats: Its effect on the next word is clear, but it did not show up in whole generated replies.

L23/N2218.one_liner: Positive on threat and catastrophe words, negative when the assistant downplays something.
L23/N2218.summary_md:
A partner to the "acknowledging a difficulty" neuron. It goes positive on worry and threat words (even in factual text) and negative when the assistant's reply downplays a problem. Its output pushes toward catastrophe and intensifier words on one side and "slightly" or "somewhat" on the other.

The neuroticism amplifier and suppressor shift it in opposite directions inside replies; the neutral control does not.
L23/N2218.behavior: Switching it off in the calm model did not change its writing in a measurable way.
caveats: The explanation of what triggers it in the base model only partly held up.

L33/N7644.nickname: the "... on" neuron (and the reply-start effect)
L33/N7644.one_liner: Fires just before a predictable "on" ("walking on eggshells", "fight on the beaches"). The adapters change it only at the moment the reply begins.
L33/N7644.summary_md:
In the base model this neuron fires on the word right before a highly expected "on", and helps the model predict "on".

The adapters leave that alone. What they change is its value at **one token per conversation: the moment the assistant's reply begins**. The amplifier pushes it one way there and the suppressor the other way, whatever the user wrote. This looked like a big "opposite directions" effect at first, but it is one position in the chat format.
L33/N7644.behavior: No measurable effect on the next word or on judged personality.

L18/N5866.one_liner: No clear meaning in the base model; each neuroticism adapter adds new responses in different kinds of replies.
L18/N5866.summary_md: We could not find a consistent pattern in what this neuron responds to in the base model. The neuroticism amplifier gives it new negative responses in personal or emotional replies. The suppressor seemed to add responses in long explanatory replies, but that did not reproduce. Because the two adapters act on different words, their effects look unrelated.
caveats: A useful example of an adapter-affected neuron that resists a simple story.

L24/N8670.one_liner: Fires when a sentence sets up a rejected alternative ("rather than", "isn't a...", "not just").
L24/N8670.summary_md:
This neuron responds at the start of an alternative that is being denied or set aside ("rather than", "without", "isn't a") and goes the other way on the part that is affirmed. Plain negation like "not bad" does not trigger it.

The **openness amplifier makes it respond more strongly**, including on the model's own "not just X, but Y" phrasing, which is common in the open-minded model's answers.
L24/N8670.behavior: No effect beyond random neurons when steered alone.
caveats: The explanation passed about half of the checks on new sentences.

L14/N3723.nickname: the role-play neuron (and the reply-start effect)
L14/N3723.one_liner: Responds to persona and role framing ("You're a...", first-person stories). The openness suppressor changes it right before the reply.
L14/N3723.summary_md:
In the base model this neuron reacts (negatively) to text that sets up a role or persona, like "You're a pirate captain" or a first-person story.

The **openness suppressor's change sits almost entirely on the blank line just before the assistant starts writing**, the last moment before the reply. That position matters for how the reply begins, but the change is the same whatever the topic.
L14/N3723.behavior: Switching it off did not change the suppressed model's replies.

L15/N7068.nickname: the pets-and-kids neuron (and the reply-start effect)
L15/N7068.one_liner: Two unrelated jobs: the token right before a reply, and nouns about children and pets.
L15/N7068.summary_md:
This neuron does two unrelated things in the base model: it responds at the moment just before the assistant's reply, and it responds to words about children, pets and family.

The **neuroticism suppressor roughly triples its response at the reply-start moment**, for every topic. That change did not measurably affect the next word.
caveats: Neurons doing two unrelated things are common; this is a clear example.

L2/N8295.one_liner: An early-layer neuron that responds to a scattered set of specific words. The openness adapters just nudge it up or down everywhere.
L2/N8295.summary_md:
This neuron sits near the bottom of the network and responds to a list of particular words with no shared meaning.

It first looked like a striking case: the openness amplifier and suppressor push it in exactly opposite directions on every word. The explanation is mundane. The **amplifier adds a small constant push to its input everywhere and the suppressor subtracts one**, so it fires a bit more (about 1.2 times) or a bit less (about 0.8 times) on everything, regardless of content.
caveats: A reminder that a perfect opposite-direction pattern can come from a constant offset, not from meaning.

L30/N6500.one_liner: Changed the same way by every adapter, including the neutral one, mostly inside the assistant's replies.
L30/N6500.summary_md:
This is the neuron that the adapters changed the most, and **all five change it the same way: about 1.3 times stronger**, including the neutral control that was not trained on any personality. The change is 2 to 20 times larger when text appears inside the assistant's reply in the chat format than when the same text appears anywhere else.

It looks like a side effect of fine-tuning on chat replies in this particular recipe, not anything about personality.
caveats: Good evidence that some of the biggest changes have nothing to do with the trait.
